# Introduction
While the first data center was opened in 1946 @[Tozzi2026], it was not until the 2000s that data centers started to become common. Furthermore, it has only been a handful of years since an explosion occurred in both the construction and scale of new data centers due to the widespread adoption of LLMs. This growth has led to a dramatic increase in the amount of energy and water used, the space needed for these developments, and the potential economic impact @[Schulz2025]. Most of the public discourse and recent research on data centers revolve around the impacts on energy and water. However, the economic impact on the communities surrounding these data centers has received relatively little attention to date.

The primary limiting factor preventing research is a lack of data on data centers. This breaks down into two sub-issues: (1) a lack of historical data, which is a natural consequence of the recent explosion in construction, and (2) a lack of complete and precise information on the timing and scale of specific data center construction. The first issue will resolve itself with time, but the second is a transparency issue systemic to the industry. Several private data aggregators, such as Aterio, Cleanview, and Data Center Map, offer approximations of the temporal and geospatial data required to research the local economic and environmental impacts of data centers, but at prices that can range into the tens of thousands of dollars.

Our paper presents a novel approach to resolving this data sourcing and consistency problem, opening the door to future research. Due to data centers’ recent surfacing in the public consciousness, misconceptions have started to calcify about what a “data center” is and the impact data centers have based on their placement. Our analysis clarifies these points by defining data centers strictly as those operations that meet the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) subsector code 518, which is defined as follows: “The Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web Hosting, and Related Services subsector groups establishments that provide computing infrastructure, data processing services, Web hosting services (except software publishing), and related services, including streaming support services (except streaming distribution services)” (“NAICS 518”). Using this definition provides several benefits. The first benefit is that it uses a national standard already common in economics literature, making any existing work based on this system compatible. The second, and perhaps greater, benefit is that U.S. federal statistics, such as those collected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the U.S. Census Bureau, use these codes and report consistent, historical data through them. All other currently available datasets tracking the timing and location of data center construction must invent their own operational definition of “data center” and impute which operations match that definition across hundreds or thousands of regional databases.
